content: An exanthem is a widespread rash that typically arises due to a viral infection and is most commonly observed in children. The rash can result from one of three mechanisms: a reaction to a toxin produced by the infectious organism, direct damage to the skin caused by the organism, or an immune response triggered by the infection. In some cases, exanthems may also be caused by medications, with antibiotics being the most frequent culprits. Historically, five classical childhood exanthems have been identified. These include measles (rubeola), chickenpox (varicella), rubella, scarlet fever, and fifth disease (erythema infectiosum). A sixth condition, roseola (also known as exanthem subitum or sixth disease), was later added to this list. Vaccines are now available for measles, rubella, and chickenpox, significantly reducing their prevalence. Scarlet fever, which is caused by a streptococcal bacterial infection, is easily treatable with antibiotics. The remaining two viral syndromes, fifth disease and roseola, are generally considered benign and self-limiting. In 1992, a new exanthem was identified and named unilateral laterothoracic exanthem (ULE). This condition is also referred to as asymmetric periflexural exanthem of childhood.
